title: Containers at five ports
intro: The bar chart shows the total cargo, in million tonnes, handled by five ports, P, Q, R, S and T, in 2023 and 2024. The table shows the percentage of each port's total cargo that was containerised in each of the two years.
All cargo at a port that is not containerised is bulk cargo.

Additional information for questions 4 and 5: in 2025, each port is expected to handle exactly as much total cargo as in 2024. The port authority wants the containerised cargo of the five ports together to be at least half of their combined cargo. No port's containerised share can fall below its 2024 level or rise by more than 10 percentage points above it.

data.caption: Containerised cargo as a percentage of total cargo

questions.stem: Which port recorded the largest increase in containerised cargo, in million tonnes, from 2023 to 2024?
why: Containerised cargo is total cargo × share. 2023 to 2024: P 51.2 to 52.5, Q 29.4 to 43.2, R 76.0 to 79.2, S 12.8 to 25.6, T 55.2 to 52.47.
The increases: Q 13.8, S 12.8, R 3.2, P 1.3; T fell. Q is the largest.
The trap is S: its share rose the most (12 points) and its containerised cargo doubled, but from a smaller base, so the increase in tonnes is smaller.

questions.stem: By approximately what percentage did the bulk cargo handled by the five ports together increase from 2023 to 2024?
why: Total cargo: 520 in 2023 and 559 in 2024. Containerised cargo: 224.6 in 2023 and 252.97 in 2024.
5.7% averages the five ports' bulk growth rates, which ignores their sizes; 7.5% is the growth of total cargo and 12.6% that of containerised cargo.

questions.stem: For how many of the five ports was the percentage change in containerised cargo from 2023 to 2024 greater than the percentage change in the port's total cargo?
why: The percentage change in a part is greater than that in its whole exactly when the part's share of the whole rises, so no multiplication is needed.
The share rose at Q (35 to 45), R (50 to 55) and S (20 to 32), and fell at P and T. That is 3 ports.
R is the one to watch: its total cargo fell by 5.3% while its containerised cargo rose by 4.2%, and +4.2% is greater than −5.3%.

questions.stem: If the containerised cargo of the five ports together is exactly half of their combined cargo in 2025, and the containerised shares of P and T stay at their 2024 levels, what is the minimum possible containerised share of port R in 2025, in per cent, to the nearest integer?
why: Half of 559 is 279.5. Containerised cargo in 2024 was 252.97, so the five ports must add 26.53 million tonnes.
P and T add nothing. Q and S can add at most 10 points of their cargo: 9.6 and 8.0, together 17.6.
To keep R as low as possible, Q and S add their most, and R adds the rest: 26.53 − 17.6 = 8.93, within R's own limit of 14.4.
R's containerised cargo is then 79.2 + 8.93 = 88.13 out of 144, a share of 61.2%, which is 61 to the nearest integer.

questions.stem: What is the smallest number of ports whose containerised share needs to rise for the authority's target to be met?
why: Half of 559 is 279.5. Containerised cargo in 2024 was 252.97, so it must rise by at least 26.53 million tonnes.
A port can add at most 10% of its total cargo: R 14.4, P 14.0, T 9.9, Q 9.6, S 8.0.
One port is not enough (R alone adds 14.4). The two largest, R and P, can add 28.4, which covers 26.53. So 2.

steps: Turn the two charts into one table first: containerised cargo = total cargo × share. 2023: P 51.2, Q 29.4, R 76.0, S 12.8, T 55.2 (224.6 in all). 2024: P 52.5, Q 43.2, R 79.2, S 25.6, T 52.47 (252.97 in all).
Bulk cargo is the rest: 295.4 in 2023 and 306.03 in 2024, out of totals of 520 and 559.
A part's percentage change is greater than its whole's exactly when its share rises: read that straight off the table, without multiplying.

For the 2025 questions, turn every limit into tonnes: the target is 279.5, so 26.53 more is needed, and a port can add at most 10% of its cargo (R 14.4, P 14.0, T 9.9, Q 9.6, S 8.0). For the fewest ports, use the biggest first; for the least at one port, let the others add their most.

title: Six economies: income, growth and size
cite: World Bank, World Development Indicators, 2023 (GDP per head in current US$, real GDP growth, GDP in current US$), as tabulated by StatisticsTimes; CC BY 4.0. GDP per head rounded to US$ 10, growth to 0.1 point. Population is GDP ÷ GDP per head, rounded to the nearest million (derived, not a published figure). The questions are ours.
intro: The scatter chart plots six economies by GDP per head in 2023 (across, in US$) and real GDP growth in 2023 (up, in %). The table gives the plotted values and each economy's population.
Use the figures printed here. A country's total GDP is its GDP per head × its population (US$, nominal).

Additional information for questions 3 to 5: the printed figures are for the end of 2023. From then on, each country's total GDP and GDP per head (in US$) both grow every year at the growth rate shown for it, compounded annually, and its population does not change. So a figure for the end of 2023 + n is the 2023 figure after n years of growth.

data.caption: GDP per head (US$), growth (%) and population (million), 2023

questions.stem: The combined GDP of all the countries whose GDP per head is below US$ 5,000 is what percentage of China's GDP? Give your answer to the nearest integer.
why: Below US$ 5,000: India, Indonesia, Vietnam and Bangladesh. Their totals (US$ billion): India 2,530 × 1,438 = 3,638; Indonesia 4,880 × 281 = 1,371; Vietnam 4,320 × 100 = 432; Bangladesh 2,550 × 172 = 439. Sum 5,880.

questions.stem: Call a country a 'catch-up economy' if its growth rate is higher than the growth rate of every country that has a higher GDP per head than it. (The country with the highest GDP per head is not counted.) How many of the six are catch-up economies?
why: Richest first, with growth: China 5.4, Brazil 3.2, Indonesia 5.0, Vietnam 5.1, Bangladesh 5.8, India 9.2.
Brazil, Indonesia and Vietnam each grow slower than China (5.4), so none of them qualifies. Bangladesh's 5.8 beats all four richer countries, and India's 9.2 beats all five. So 2.
4 compares each country only with the next richer one: Indonesia (5.0 > 3.2) and Vietnam (5.1 > 5.0) then pass too.

questions.stem: By the end of which year will India's total GDP first be at least one-third of China's total GDP?
why: India ÷ China now = 3,638 ÷ 18,260 = 0.1992. Each year the ratio is multiplied by 1.092 ÷ 1.054 = 1.0361.
0.1992 needs to grow by 1/3 ÷ 0.1992 = 1.673 times. After 14 years the ratio is 0.327, after 15 years 0.339. So 15 years: the end of 2038.

2039 comes from comparing GDP per head (2,530 ÷ 12,950 = 0.195) instead of total GDP, which needs one more year. 2037 comes from growing at the difference of the rates, 3.8% a year, which overstates the gain.

questions.stem: By what percentage will Bangladesh's total GDP exceed Vietnam's total GDP at the end of 2028? Give your answer to the nearest integer.
why: Today Bangladesh is 438.6 and Vietnam 432.0 (US$ billion): Bangladesh is already 1.5% ahead.

questions.stem: By the end of which year will each of India, Indonesia, Vietnam and Bangladesh have a GDP per head of at least US$ 6,000?
why: Years each needs: Indonesia 5 (4,880 → 6,228), Vietnam 7, India 10, Bangladesh 16 (2,550 × 1.058¹⁵ = 5,940, × 1.058¹⁶ = 6,285).
All four are there only when the last, Bangladesh, is: 2023 + 16 = 2039.

2033 is India's year: the poorest country on the chart is not the last to arrive, because it grows fastest. 2038 stops at 15 years, when Bangladesh is still 1% short. 2040 counts 2024 as the first of the 16 years and adds one too many.

steps: Total GDP = GDP per head × population. In US$ billion: India 3,638, China 18,260, Brazil 2,190, Indonesia 1,371, Vietnam 432, Bangladesh 439.
Growth questions compare ratios: a ratio of two countries' GDP changes each year by (1 + one rate) ÷ (1 + the other), so one multiplication a year on the calculator is enough.
For 'the first year', find the last year short of the mark and the first year past it; the options are a year apart.

title: India's goods trade with five partners
cite: Department of Commerce, Government of India, DGCIS Quick Estimates, country-wise merchandise exports and imports, released by PIB, July 2026; US$ million converted to US$ billion, exports rounded to 0.1 billion, imports as % of exports to the nearest whole percent. Financial years run April to March. The questions are ours.
intro: The first bar chart shows India's merchandise exports to five partners in 2024-25 and 2025-26. The second shows India's imports from each partner as a percentage of its exports to that partner, in the same two years.

Use the rounded figures printed here. Imports from a partner in a year = exports to that partner × the percentage shown for that year. The trade deficit with a partner is imports − exports, and the trade surplus is exports − imports. All amounts are in US$ billion.

data.caption: Imports as a percentage of exports

questions.stem: What was India's combined trade deficit in 2025-26 with the four partners with which it had a deficit in that year (in US$ billion)? Give your answer to the nearest integer.
why: Imports in 2025-26 = exports × percentage: China 19.5 × 6.76 = 131.82, UAE 37.4 × 1.71 = 63.95, Saudi Arabia 10.3 × 2.99 = 30.80, Singapore 11.9 × 2.04 = 24.28. The USA's percentage is below 100, so it is a surplus partner.
Deficits: China 112.32, UAE 26.55, Saudi Arabia 20.50, Singapore 12.38. Sum 171.75, so 172.

questions.stem: Among China, UAE, Saudi Arabia and Singapore, with which one did India's trade deficit increase by the largest percentage from 2024-25 to 2025-26?
why: Deficit = exports × (percentage − 100%). Singapore 8.32 → 12.38 (+49%); China 99.53 → 112.32 (+13%); Saudi Arabia 18.41 → 20.50 (+11%); UAE 26.72 → 26.55 (a small fall).
China's deficit rose by the most in US$ (12.8 billion), but Singapore's rose by the largest percentage.

questions.stem: India's net balance with the five partners together is its total exports to them minus its total imports from them; it was negative in both years. By approximately what percentage did India's net deficit with the five partners together increase from 2024-25 to 2025-26?
why: The net deficit rose from 112.32 to 137.70: 25.38 ÷ 112.32 = 22.6%, so 23%.
12% leaves out the USA, whose surplus shrank; 11% is the growth of total imports alone; 18% divides the rise by the later year's deficit.

questions.stem: For how many of the five partners did India's imports rise from 2024-25 to 2025-26 even though imports as a percentage of exports fell?
why: The percentage fell only for China (796 → 676) and the UAE (173 → 171).
0 reads a falling percentage as falling imports; the percentage is a ratio, and exports changed too.

questions.stem: Had imports from China in 2025-26 been unchanged but the trade deficit with China been 40% lower than it actually was, by approximately what percentage would exports to China have exceeded their actual 2025-26 value?
why: Actual deficit 112.32. 40% lower means 112.32 × 0.6 = 67.39. Imports stay 131.82, so exports would be 131.82 − 67.39 = 64.43.
64.43 ÷ 19.5 = 3.30: exports would be 230% higher.
70% divides the rise of 44.93 by the new exports (64.43) instead of the actual ones; 346% cuts the deficit to 40% of its size instead of by 40%; 40% applies the cut to exports.

steps: Imports = exports × percentage. 2024-25: USA 45.85, China 113.83, UAE 63.32, Saudi Arabia 30.21, Singapore 21.32. 2025-26: USA 53.25, China 131.82, UAE 63.95, Saudi Arabia 30.80, Singapore 24.28.
Deficit = imports − exports, or exports × (percentage − 100%). A percentage below 100 is a surplus (the USA).
The second chart is a ratio: when it falls, imports can still rise if exports rose faster.

title: India's installed power capacity, three years
cite: Central Electricity Authority, 'Growth of electricity sector in India', as cited in the CERC Market Monitoring Report 2023-24, chapter 1; installed capacity at the end of each financial year. Renewables' shares computed from the same figures. The questions are ours.
intro: The stacked bar chart shows India's installed electricity capacity by source at the end of three financial years, with solar, wind and Other RE (small hydro and bio-power) shown together as renewables. The second chart splits each year's renewable capacity between solar, wind and Other RE.

Use the figures printed here. Total capacity in a year is the sum of the four parts of its bar. 'Hydro (large)' excludes small hydro. A source's capacity within renewables is the renewable capacity × its share. The shares are rounded, so they may not add up to exactly 100.

questions.stem: By what percentage did India's solar capacity increase from 2021-22 to 2023-24? Give your answer to the nearest integer.
why: Dividing the shares alone (57.0 ÷ 49.1, 16%) misses that renewables themselves grew.

questions.stem: For how many of the six sources (solar, wind, Other RE, large hydro, nuclear and thermal) did capacity rise in both 2022-23 and 2023-24 while its share of total capacity fell in both years? (Capacity that did not change in a year did not rise.)
why: Solar (13.5% → 16.1% → 18.5%) and wind (10.1% → 10.3% → 10.4%) gained share; nuclear did not grow in 2022-23. So 3: thermal, large hydro and Other RE.
Other RE is the trap both ways: its share of renewables fell every year, which looks like a fall in capacity, but its capacity rose.

questions.stem: Suppose that from 2023-24 onwards, solar capacity adds each year exactly the amount it added in 2023-24, and thermal capacity also adds each year exactly the amount it added in 2023-24. What is the least number of years (after 2023-24) after which solar capacity will exceed thermal capacity?
why: 2023-24 additions: solar 81.87 − 66.83 = 15.04 GW; thermal 243.22 − 237.27 = 5.95 GW. The gap, 243.22 − 81.87 = 161.35 GW, closes by 9.09 GW a year.
161.35 ÷ 9.09 = 17.7: after 17 years thermal is still ahead, after 18 solar leads. So 18.
11 ignores thermal's additions; 16 uses the average additions of the two years; 14 uses the 2022-23 additions.

questions.stem: Suppose solar capacity in 2023-24 had been the same as in 2021-22, with wind and Other RE as they actually were in 2023-24. What would solar's share of the combined capacity of solar, wind and Other RE have been in 2023-24?
why: 37.6% divides by the actual 2023-24 renewables (143.64), which still include the actual solar; 19.4% is the fall in solar as a share of renewables; 13.5% is solar's 2021-22 share of all capacity.

questions.stem: With thermal, large hydro and nuclear capacity kept at their 2023-24 levels, what additional capacity (in GW) of solar, wind and Other RE together would make these three exactly 40% of the total installed capacity? Give your answer to the nearest integer.
why: The rest is 243.22 + 46.93 + 8.18 = 298.33 GW, and must be 60% of the new total. So renewables must be 298.33 × 40 ÷ 60 = 198.89 GW.
Taking 40% of today's total (441.97) gives 176.79 and 33 GW, but the total grows as renewables are added.

steps: A falling share of renewables is not falling capacity: Other RE's share fell every year while its capacity rose, because renewables grew.

title: Three streaming platforms: subscriber growth
intro: The line chart shows the year-on-year growth, in per cent, in the subscribers of three streaming platforms, Aarav, Bhava and Chitra, in each year from 2020 to 2024. The table gives each platform's subscribers, in millions, in 2019.
A platform's subscribers in a year = its subscribers in the previous year × (1 + that year's growth rate). Use the printed rates exactly.

questions.stem: In how many of the 15 platform-years (three platforms in each of the five years from 2020 to 2024) did a platform add at least 10 million subscribers over the previous year?
why: At least 10 million: Aarav's first three years and all five of Chitra's, so 8.
Counting growth rates of 10% or more gives 11 instead: a high rate on a small base adds few subscribers.

questions.stem: Between 2019 and 2024, whose share of the three platforms' combined subscribers changed the least, in percentage points, whichever way it moved?
options: Bhava and Chitra, by the same amount
why: Subscribers in 2024: Aarav 92.8, Bhava 75.2, Chitra 109.3 million, 277.3 in all (120 in 2019).
Shares, 2019 to 2024: Aarav 33.3% to 33.5%, Bhava 45.8% to 27.1%, Chitra 20.8% to 39.4%. Aarav moves by 0.1 points, Bhava by 18.7 and Chitra by 18.6.
Aarav grew 2.32 times, almost exactly as fast as the three together (2.31 times), so its share hardly moved.

questions.stem: In how many of the five years from 2020 to 2024 was the growth rate of the three platforms' combined subscribers higher than the simple average of their three growth rates that year?
why: The combined rate is an average weighted by each platform's subscribers at the start of the year, so it beats the simple average only when the faster growers are the larger ones.
Combined against simple average: 2020 27.92% against 34.67%; 2021 24.95% against 27.00%; 2022 14.54% against 15.33%; 2023 13.77% against 13.33%; 2024 10.94% against 10.67%.
Higher in 2023 and 2024 only: by then Chitra, the fastest grower, is the largest platform.

questions.stem: Suppose Bhava's growth in 2022 had been +8% instead of −4%, and Chitra's growth in 2023 had been +15% instead of +22%, with every other rate unchanged. By what percentage would the three platforms' combined subscribers in 2024 have differed from the actual figure? Enter a positive number if higher and a negative one if lower, correct to one decimal place.
why: A changed rate scales that year's figure and every later one by the same factor. Bhava's 2024 figure × (1.08 ÷ 0.96 = 1.125): 75.16 to 84.55 million. Chitra's × (1.15 ÷ 1.22 = 0.9426): 109.34 to 103.07.
Aarav stays at 92.78. Combined: 280.40 against 277.27, 1.13% higher, so 1.1.
Adding the changes in percentage points (+12 and −7) cannot work: the two changes act on different bases.

questions.stem: In the same case (Bhava +8% in 2022, Chitra +15% in 2023, every other rate unchanged), Chitra's net addition of subscribers from 2019 to 2024 would have been what percentage of the three platforms' combined net addition over the same years?
why: In that case Chitra reaches 103.07 million, a net addition of 78.07; the three together reach 280.40, a net addition of 160.40.
54% is the actual share, without the changes; 37% is Chitra's share of the combined 2024 total, not of the additions.

steps: Build each platform's subscribers year by year from 2019, multiplying by 1 + the year's rate. 2024: Aarav 92.78, Bhava 75.16, Chitra 109.34 million.
A combined growth rate needs the subscribers, not the rates: it is weighted by each platform's size.
In a what-if, a changed rate rescales that year and every later year by the new factor ÷ the old one.

title: A diversified group: segment revenue and profit
intro: A diversified group has five segments. The pie chart shows each segment's share of the group's revenue in 2025. The table shows each segment's revenue growth from 2024 to 2025 and its operating margin in each of the two years.
The Finance segment's operating profit in 2025 was ₹ 4,320 crore. The pie's shares are exact.
A segment's operating profit = its revenue × its operating margin; a negative margin is a loss. The group's operating margin = its total operating profit ÷ its total revenue.

questions.stem: By what percentage did the group's total revenue grow from 2024 to 2025? Give your answer correct to one decimal place.
why: Finance's 2025 revenue = 4,320 ÷ 0.40 = ₹ 10,800 crore, which is 9% of the group: the group's 2025 revenue = 10,800 ÷ 0.09 = ₹ 1,20,000 crore.

Segments in 2025: Retail 40,800, Telecom 30,000, Energy 24,000, Media 14,400, Finance 10,800. Dividing each by 1 + its growth gives 2024: 34,000, 25,000, 30,000, 9,000 and 10,000, which is 1,08,000 in all.

questions.stem: The group's operating profit rose from 2024 to 2025. Split the rise into two parts. The volume part is the sum, over the segments, of (the change in the segment's revenue) × (its 2024 margin). The margin part is the sum, over the segments, of (its 2025 revenue) × (the change in its margin from 2024 to 2025). What was the margin part, in ₹ crore? Give your answer to the nearest integer.
why: Margin part, segment by segment (2025 revenue × change in margin): Retail 40,800 × −2% = −816; Telecom 30,000 × 3% = 900; Energy 24,000 × −3% = −720; Media 14,400 × 7% = 1,008; Finance 10,800 × 2% = 216. Sum: 588.
Check: the volume part is 1,036, and 1,036 + 588 = 1,624, the whole rise in operating profit.
Using 2024 revenue in the margin part gives 0, and the two parts then no longer add up to the rise.

questions.stem: Leave the Media segment out altogether, both its revenue and its loss. What would the operating margin of the other four segments together have been in 2025, in per cent? Give your answer to the nearest integer.
why: 2025 operating profit, ₹ crore: Retail 3,264, Telecom 10,500, Energy 2,880, Finance 4,320, and Media −720, a loss.
Without Media: 20,964 of profit on 1,20,000 − 14,400 = 1,05,600 of revenue, a margin of 19.85%, so 20.
With Media the group's margin is 16.9%: leaving out a loss-making segment raises the margin through both profit and revenue.

questions.stem: By what percentage did the group's total operating profit change from 2024 to 2025?
why: 2024 operating profit, ₹ crore: Retail 3,400, Telecom 8,000, Energy 4,500, Media −1,080, Finance 3,800; 18,620 in all. 2025: 20,244.
Revenue grew 11.1%, but margins moved: the group's margin fell from 17.2% to 16.9%, so profit grew more slowly.

questions.stem: Suppose the Energy segment's 2025 revenue had stayed at its 2024 level, with its 2025 margin and every other segment unchanged. What would the group's 2025 operating margin have been?
why: Energy's revenue would be 30,000 instead of 24,000, and its profit 12% × 30,000 = 3,600 instead of 2,880.
The group: 20,964 of profit on 1,26,000 of revenue, a margin of 16.64%, so 16.6%.
16.1% keeps Energy's old profit with its new revenue.

steps: Start from the one figure in rupees: Finance's profit and margin give its revenue, and its 9% share gives the group's, ₹ 1,20,000 crore in 2025.
The shares give each segment's 2025 revenue; dividing by 1 + growth gives 2024; × the margins gives the profits in both years.
The margin of a total is its profit ÷ its revenue, never an average of the segments' margins.

title: Six regions: leads, conversion and deal size
intro: The bar chart shows the number of sales leads, in thousands, that a company generated in each of six regions in a year. The scatter chart shows, for each region, its conversion rate (the percentage of leads that became deals, across) and its average deal size (up), in ₹ lakh.
Deals = leads × conversion rate. Revenue = deals × average deal size. As 1 crore = 100 lakh, a region's revenue in ₹ crore = leads (thousand) × conversion rate (%) × deal size (₹ lakh) ÷ 10.

data.caption: Conversion rate and average deal size

questions.stem: Rank the six regions by leads (1 for the most) and again by revenue (1 for the highest). For how many regions do the two ranks differ by 2 or more?
why: Revenue, ₹ crore: North 120.0, South 162.0, East 96.0, West 208.0, Central 186.2, North-East 178.2.
Ranks by leads: North 1, West 2, South 3, Central 4, East 5, North-East 6. By revenue: West 1, Central 2, North-East 3, South 4, North 5, East 6.
Gaps: North 4, North-East 3, Central 2; South, East and West 1 each. So 3.

questions.stem: Take the regions whose conversion rate is above the company's overall conversion rate (its total deals ÷ its total leads) and whose average deal size is below the simple average of the six regions' deal sizes. What was their combined revenue, in ₹ crore? Give your answer correct to one decimal place.
why: Deals: North 2,400, South 2,700, East 2,400, West 2,600, Central 2,660, North-East 1,980; 14,740 on 2,47,000 leads, an overall rate of 5.97%.
Above 5.97%: South (6), East (8), Central (7) and North-East (9). The average deal size is ₹ 6.5 lakh; below it, of these: South (6) and East (4).
Revenue: 162.0 + 96.0 = 258.0. The simple average of the six rates (6.5%) would drop South and give 96.0.

questions.stem: The company wants every region to earn at least ₹ 150 crore. Leads and deal sizes cannot change; a region below ₹ 150 crore may raise its conversion rate as far as it needs, but by at most 3 percentage points. After that, what is the total shortfall below ₹ 150 crore across the regions, in ₹ crore? Give your answer to the nearest integer.
why: Below ₹ 150 crore: North (120.0) and East (96.0).
North needs a rate of 150 × 10 ÷ (60 × 5) = 5.0%, one point more: it reaches 150, no shortfall.
East needs 12.5%, 4.5 points more, but may add only 3: at 11.0% it earns 30 × 11 × 4 ÷ 10 = 132.0, 18 short. The total shortfall is 18.

questions.stem: Suppose North-East had doubled its leads, to 44 thousand, while its conversion rate fell by 1 percentage point, to 8%, with every other region unchanged. What would the company's overall conversion rate (total deals ÷ total leads) have been?
why: In all: 16,280 deals on 2,69,000 leads = 6.05%.
Keeping North-East at 9% gives 6.22%; the simple average of the six new rates is 6.33%.

questions.stem: The company moves 10 thousand leads out of the region with the lowest revenue per lead. The region with the highest revenue per lead can take at most 6 thousand of them; the other 4 thousand go to the region with the second-highest revenue per lead. Each region keeps its conversion rate and deal size. By how many ₹ crore does the company's revenue rise? Give your answer correct to one decimal place.
why: Revenue per thousand leads, ₹ crore (conversion × deal size ÷ 10): North 2.0, South 3.6, East 3.2, West 4.0, Central 4.9, North-East 8.1.
From North (2.0): 6 thousand to North-East (8.1) and 4 thousand to Central (4.9).

steps: Neither chart answers alone: revenue = leads (bar) × conversion × deal size (scatter) ÷ 10.
A company-wide rate is total deals ÷ total leads, weighted by leads; it is not the average of the six rates.
Revenue per lead (conversion × deal size) decides where an extra lead earns the most.
